newsitem.title: USA: DLR ENDS LOWER ON PROFIT TAKING, BARSHEFSKY IN US.
newsitem.headline: DLR ENDS LOWER ON PROFIT TAKING, BARSHEFSKY IN US.

text.p: The dollar ended broadly lower in the U.S. after surrendering its early gains to profit-taking and signs of rising U.S.-Japanese trade tensions, dealers said.

Dealers cited persistent fears of intervention by German and Japanese central banks near current levels plus hawkish comments from U.S. Trade Representive Charlene Barshefsky over Japan's persistent trade surplus for the dollar's backsliding.
"The odds the market places on central bank intervention go up dramatically" near 1.90 marks, said Richard Vullo, vice president at Bayerische Hypobank in New York.
Dealers noted the dollar has followed a roller-coaster pattern for the last several sessions--peaking in late European trade before fading in U.S. trade.
"Europe is a bit more bullish on the dollar than the U.S.," said Vullo. "A lot of European fund managers are still moving money out of Europe."

The dollar hit a fresh 94-month high at 1.8913 marks overnight but slid steadily lower, ending at 1.8820/30, down from 1.8860/70 at the open. Dollar/yen also hit a fresh three-month high at 119.58, but ended lower at 118.69/74 versus 119.46/51 at the open.
The dollar gained in early trade against the yen when Japan's Vice Finance Minister Takeshi Komura told Reuters low Japanese interest rates were helping Japan's economy.

But the dollar later slumped when Barshefsky told reporters in Washington that U.S. officials were concerned that car exports to Japan had decreased and the trade deficit with Japan in general was deteriorating.
Japan overnight reported its customs-cleared trade surplus rose 126 percent in the first 20 days of July versus the same period a year earlier.
"That's a very short-term window, but it caused people to express concern and that's why the dollar came off," said Seth Garrett, chief dealer at Credit Suisse First Boston.
Germany Wednesday reported its jobless rate rose to 11.5 percent in July, exceeding expectations and dimming prospects for higher German interest rates, dealers said.

The Bundesbank has recently encouraged speculation it would raise interest rates if the dollar's strength persisted, but on Tuesday it made a surprisingly large injection of funds into the German money market, signalling it had no intention of raising rates for now, dealers said.
Higher rates tend to strengthen a currency by increasing returns on investments denominated in that currency.
A German government spokesman also said the dollar's rise was driven by impulsive speculation and that Germany saw no reason to change its foreign exchange stance.
"The market is blindly buying dollars. Those German numbers underscore what should be continuing bullish sentiment for the dollar," said Diego Giurleo, vice president at Royal Bank of Canada.
But profit-taking hampered the dollar as U.S. investors refused to buy the greenback at the highs, dealers noted.
"The market is telling us it is very long and is deeply concerned about a correction that could be significant. But the tone hasn't changed--it's still bid," Giurleo said.
"Of course there's always the fear of intervention, but I just don't see the rest of the world moving away from dollars at this time," he added.

The dollar fell to 1.5320/30 Swiss francs from 1.5345/55 at the open. Sterling was up at $1.6028/38 from $1.5958/63. The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3870/75 from C$1.3826/31. The Australian dollar rose to $0.7353/58 from $0.7350/55. ((--Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664))
